result:
The proposed answer of 210 is wrong.

The proof has a flaw. After the operation on the square at rows and columns $k, k+1$, the black region is not a full $(k+1)\times(k+1)$ block. Cells $(k+1,j)$ for $j<k$ and $(j,k+1)$ for $j<k$ were outside the $k\times k$ block and remain white. The induction step does not go through.

The claim that every $n$ works is also false. Take $n=3$. Only the top-left $2\times2$ square contains the initial black cell, so that move is forced and colours $(1,2),(2,1),(2,2)$ black. The only square now with exactly one black cell is the bottom-right one, at rows 2–3 and columns 2–3, which colours $(2,3),(3,2),(3,3)$ black. At that point the only white cells are $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$. Every remaining $2\times2$ square has either four black cells or three black cells, so no move is possible. The board cannot be fully coloured, and $n=3$ is excluded.

Since 3 is excluded, the set of valid $n$ is not all positive integers, so the sum $1+\cdots+20$ does not apply. I believe the known criterion is that $n$ works exactly when $3\nmid n$, which would give a sum of 300 for the smallest 20 valid values. I have not verified that criterion in general, but the rejection does not depend on it.

VERDICT: REJECT
CONFIDENCE: 5
